newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Inflation, rates to fall - Sri Lanka Central Bank.
newsitem.headline: Inflation, rates to fall - Sri Lanka Central Bank.

text.p: Sri Lanka Central Bank governor A.S. Jayawardena said on Friday he expected inflation and interest rates to fall substantially in 1997.
The government, fighting an ethnic war against Tamil separatists, was likely to ease defence spending in 1997, which would help rein in the budget deficit, he told Reuters.

"I think we should be there, more or less trying to get the inflation down, which is our main problem, running at 15 to 16 percent now and the indications are that it will come down to single digits by the middle of next year," he said.
"So by that time, I think a lot of things will get stabilised. Somewhere by the middle of next year I think we will be out of the woods," Jayawardena said.
Asked if single-digit inflation would create the climate for interest rate cuts, Jayawardena said: "Definitely.
"The moment inflation comes down, there will be reductions all around in interest rates.

"That's the main purpose in trying to tackle inflation, to bring down the level of interest rates from present levels which are discouraging investment, and secondly to bring stability to the exchange rate."
Jayawardena said he hoped to see real interest rates for business loans at about two percent.
"In other words, if inflation is eight (percent), I would expect it (loan rates) to be around 10. Two percentage points above inflation would be ... a reasonable level of interest rates," he said.
Sri Lankan prime rates are about 17.5 percent to 20 percent and other rates range up to about 24 percent.
Jayawardena said he did not expect lower rates to spark a borrowing spree.
Despite a blowout in military spending in 1996, Jayawardena said Sri Lanka remained on track for cutting the budget deficit to 4.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product by 1999.
President Chandrika Kumaratunga's government would spend about 45 billion rupees on defence in 1996, mainly on procurement to modernise the military, he said.
"Now we don't have to repeat that next year. So in that sense, we expect a moderation in defence expenditure next year," he said.
"In that sense we would expect an easing of the budget problem," Jayawardena said.
